t: LeetCode 2208 - Minimum Operations to Halve Array Sum: Always Shrink the Current Maximum
o: **Understanding the problem.** Each operation picks one element and replaces it with exactly half of itself, possibly revisiting it later; we want the fewest operations until the array sum drops by at least half of its initial value. In Example 1 (nums = [5,19,8,1], initial sum 33, target reduction 16.5) halving 19 reclaims 9.5, halving the resulting 9.5 reclaims 4.75, and halving 8 reclaims 4 - a cumulative 18.25 in just 3 operations, and fewer cannot reach 16.5. The greedy principle is clear: the largest current element offers the largest immediate reduction, and an exchange argument shows no schedule beats it. With up to 10^5 elements and values up to 10^7, repeatedly rescanning for the maximum is too slow; a max-heap delivers each pick in logarithmic time.
k: Greedy exchange argument: replacing any non-maximum pick in an optimal schedule with the current maximum never reduces the reclaimed amount, so always halve the maximum.
Halving is geometric decay, so a single element enters the heap only O(log S) times and the total operation count stays modest.
Floating point is safe here - dividing by 2 only decrements the exponent, so values stay exactly representable; still, use doubles for the running sums.

a.n: Approach 1: Rescan for the Maximum Each Step
a.i: Simulate literally: convert to floats, and in every iteration find the largest element by a linear scan, halve it in place, and bank the reclaimed difference. Simple and obviously faithful to the greedy idea, but each of the K operations pays O(n) for the search.
s: Compute the target as half of the initial sum.
While the reclaimed amount is below target, locate the maximum element via a scan.
Add half of it to the reclaimed total and overwrite it with that half.
Count iterations and return the count.

c.python:
class Solution:
    def halveArray(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        target = sum(nums) / 2
        arr = list(map(float, nums))
        ans = reduced = 0
        while reduced < target:
            i = arr.index(max(arr))
            reduced += arr[i] / 2
            arr[i] /= 2
            ans += 1
        return ans

a.t: O(K * n) - K operations, each paying a full O(n) scan for the maximum
a.sp: O(n) - floating-point working copy of the array

a.i: A max-heap hands us the current largest element in O(log n): pop it, credit half of its value to the progress bar, and push the halved remainder back. Stop as soon as the credited total reaches half of the original sum. Correctness follows from the same exchange argument - the multiset of available halvings only depends on which element was last touched, and taking the fattest first dominates.
s: Push all elements into a max-heap and set target = sum / 2.
Pop the maximum x; add x / 2 to the accumulated reduction.
Push x / 2 back into the heap and increment the operation counter.
Terminate when the accumulated reduction >= target and return the counter.

c.python:
import heapq

class Solution:
    def halveArray(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        target = sum(nums) / 2
        heap = [-x for x in nums]
        heapq.heapify(heap)
        ans = reduced = 0
        while reduced < target:
            x = -heapq.heappop(heap)
            reduced += x / 2
            heapq.heappush(heap, -(x / 2))
            ans += 1
        return ans

a.t: O(K log n) - K operations each doing O(log n) heap work, with K = O(n log S) because every pick halves some element
a.sp: O(n) - the heap stores all elements

w: Present the greedy claim explicitly and defend it with the exchange argument before coding - that proof is the interview differentiator, the heap is just plumbing. Pitfalls: comparing against half of the ORIGINAL sum (not the evolving one); integer arithmetic truncation, which is why everything runs in doubles; Python's heapq being a min-heap (negate keys). Note the loop always terminates because reductions form a geometric series toward the target. Follow-ups: maximize the reduction after exactly k operations (identical greedy), or stream updates where a lazy-deletion heap handles value changes.
